segments.title: How George Lewis came to own Jimmie Noone's clarinet
segments.summary: Lewis explains that a Los Angeles music store lent him a clarinet that had belonged to Jimmie Noone, and he ended up buying it. It is the Selmer he still plays; he places this about 1955-56.

segments.title: Playing with a trio versus a trumpet front line
segments.summary: The interviewer asks how playing in a trio affects Lewis's style. He says it does not worry him because he plays the melody.

segments.title: New Orleans clarinetists who impressed Lewis
segments.summary: Lewis lists clarinetists he admired in New Orleans, including Charlie McCurtis, Picou, Baquet, Tio and George Boyd, and says each had a style of his own.

segments.title: White Dixieland bands and the Prima brothers
segments.summary: Lewis discusses how some white bands changed arrangements, naming Sharkey's band, Louis Prima and Leon Prima, and Kid Rena's white pupils. The ASR is badly garbled here.

segments.title: Why other players could not sound like Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Talk about Chris Kelly's trumpet style, his tone and timing, and why others who copied his frills could not sound like him.

segments.title: Clarinet and trumpet players with a good tone
segments.summary: Lewis names players with fine tone, including Noone and Charlie McCurtis, and compares Fritz's tone to Edmund Hall's.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's band and its players
segments.summary: Lewis names musicians who played with Buddy Petit's band and others around it.

segments.title: Playing in bands in the 1920s, Bunk Johnson, and Sam Dutrey's father
segments.summary: Asked when he first played, Lewis says the late 1920s, when many bands worked around Bunk Johnson. He mentions Sam Dutrey's father.

segments.title: Commuting back to New Orleans while his father was sick
segments.summary: Lewis describes coming back to work around Jackson Square after Edmund Hall left the band, with his father ill and money tight.

segments.summary: A garbled run in which Lewis lists musicians he played with, among them the Duck Winters brothers and Chris Kelly.

segments.summary: Talk about how Chris Kelly played with a silver mute and a plunger, and about recorded versions of his tunes.

segments.summary: Lewis describes playing dances where two bands faced each other across a street, with Sam Morgan's and Kid Rena's bands, and the dance hall locations.

segments.title: Pay for dance jobs
segments.summary: The interviewer asks what dance jobs paid and when they were held.

segments.title: Band battles along the advertising route
segments.summary: Lewis explains how bands advertising a dance met on the street and played against each other, and how it was decided who won.

segments.title: The St. Peter's band with Arnold DePass
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about Arnold DePass's band; Lewis names a few members in garbled text.

segments.summary: Lewis says he went out to sit in with other bands just for the love of playing, usually unpaid.

segments.summary: Discussion of whether 'cutting' contests existed and whether rivalry between players was musical or personal.

segments.title: Using his own mouthpiece
segments.summary: Lewis says he never used another player's clarinet and always needs his own mouthpiece.

segments.title: When Lewis felt he played best: the 1930s and 1940s
segments.summary: Asked to compare 1920, 1930 and the 1940s, Lewis feels he was more mature in the 1930s and kept playing in the 1940s.

segments.summary: Garbled closing talk, including a mention of a woman sitting in and of work in California.

segments.summary: Lewis recalls how long he was in school and names the schools he attended, leaving at about 12 or 13 to work.

segments.summary: Details of a mixed school, a white teacher, Professor Nelson, subjects taught, and the cost of schooling.

segments.summary: There was no music at school, Lewis says he learned little because it was too easy, and he gives his childhood address.

segments.summary: Lewis describes the role of the trombone, which supports the melody rather than leading.
